summary:
Gangwon province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, and gender identity and gender expression are not offences in civilian life. The criminalising provision that survives, Military Criminal Act article 92-6, reaches consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023. No Gangwon-specific ordinance, police practice or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is documented in these sources, so the rules a visitor meets in the province are the national ones.

Transgender people are excluded from South Korean military service altogether, and the state's sharpest documented harm to a trans person sits in that domain. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference only, not criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. That ruling is the standard applied in Gangwon, and no province-specific gender-recognition case is documented here.

Restroom access is settled in the visitor's favour at national level and no Gangwon incident contradicts it. On 2 July 2024 a court ruled, and on 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal to finalise the matter, that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed her personal rights; the award was 300,000 won against a claim of 3 million won, and the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court, Pohang branch award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom forms part of the same national standard. No specific incident in Gangwon is documented.

Practical exposure persists despite that standard. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap that shapes what recourse a trans visitor has if refused service, housing or transport. LGBTI organisations can register, though an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, with organisers later filing charges against pastors and accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people and doxing and online harassment rose. A 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern runs in one direction: courts have loosened the conditions on legal gender recognition and have twice awarded damages over restroom exclusion, while the executive has declined to write guidelines for transgender patients and no legislature has passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination statute. Gangwon inherits both halves of that pattern.

Where the sources name a province-level unit, it is Yeongdong, in a neighbouring province rather than Gangwon, that produced the surgery-free gender-recognition ruling. The absence of a Gangwon case reflects an absence of documentation rather than a demonstrated difference in how provincial courts apply the national standard.

Peer-reviewed and commission research indicates the burden is carried early and continuously: a nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented discrimination at school, work and in transition-related care. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people, which frames the environment a visitor enters: institutions function, but protection is uneven.
localsOnly:
Residents of Gangwon obtain legal gender recognition through the national court route, and since the 8 May 2024 Yeongdong ruling the surgical prerequisite no longer applies; the 24 November 2022 Supreme Court en banc decision also permits recognition for transgender people with minor children provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent. A 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

Transgender residents are excluded from military service, and the consequences of that regime were borne most severely by Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, whose discharge was ruled unjust and reversed posthumously on 7 October 2021 before the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty in March 2024.

Residents who are refused service, employment or public accommodation have no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute to invoke; recourse runs through ordinary tort and personal-rights litigation, as in the 300,000 won restroom award finalised in July 2024 and the 7 million won Daegu District Court, Pohang branch award of 2021. Complaints to the National Human Rights Commission of Korea remain available, and that body has itself pressed the Ministry of Health and Welfare for transgender hospitalisation guidelines since November 2023.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or enter a civil union and cannot jointly adopt, and LGBTI groups can register as organisations only after sustained litigation and government appeal.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a Gangwon-specific incident involving a trans visitor, a provincial ordinance on gender identity, or a provincial enforcement pattern. The absence is a gap in sourcing, not a finding that none exists.

Whether the Yeongdong gender-recognition ruling has in fact been applied by courts sitting in Gangwon is not sourced here; the claim that it is the operative standard is an inference from national applicability.

Restroom and facilities conditions in Gangwon's hotels, restaurants, transport hubs and public buildings are not covered by any source in this inventory, and no province-level data on hate-crime incidents against trans people is available.

The inventory does not establish whether Gangwon's healthcare providers have adopted any transgender-sensitive hospitalisation practice following the November 2023 National Human Rights Commission of Korea finding, and no reporting on the Ministry of Health and Welfare's position since that rejection is included.

Police responsiveness to anti-LGBT violence in Gangwon is not sourced; the documented cases of police inaction concern Pride events in other cities.
